title: Commuting permutations with few joint orbits: asymptotics, log-concavity and the density of failures in every rank
shortTitle: Commuting permutations: where log-concavity fails, in every rank
oneLine: Abdesselam's conjecture fails at two orbits in every rank, holds at every fixed larger orbit count, and the failures have a density
abstract: Count the ordered ℓ-tuples of pairwise commuting permutations of n objects that have exactly k joint orbits. For a single permutation these are the Stirling numbers, which are log-concave in k; Abdesselam conjectured log-concavity for every ℓ and n. Starr (2026) showed at rank two that it fails at k = 2 for infinitely many n but holds at every fixed k ≥ 3 for large n, and Charlton, Heim and Stumpenhusen found the first rank-two failure, n = 65 214 507 758 400. This candidate treats every fixed rank ℓ ≥ 2 and fixed k: an asymptotic formula with an Euler-product arithmetic factor and an explicit error uniform in the factorisation of n; failure at k = 2 in every rank (the ratio tends to 0 along n = m! and is below any ε on a set of positive density); log-concavity for large n at every fixed k ≥ 3, with the exact limit inferior and superior as Euler products (about 2.52 at ℓ = 3, k = 3, against the elementary bound 1.10); a continuous limiting distribution, so the density of two-orbit failures exists and lies strictly between 0 and 1 in every rank, new also at rank two; and certified explicit failures with 54 digits in rank three and 845 digits in rank four. Limits: fixed orbit counts only; the leading term follows the classical Ingham–Halberstam route and the density applies the Erdős–Wintner theorem; the explicit failures are not claimed minimal. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

evidence: A 20-page paper with a plain introduction (the question, what was known, what is new, why two orbits are exceptional, methods and a roadmap), written proofs of every theorem, checks, scope, open problems and an AI-use statement. Two Python programs (mpmath 1.3.0) accompany it: verify.py (brute-force enumeration of commuting tuples against the coefficient formula, exact convolution identities through n = 40, every rational constant, the asymptotic formula against exact counts up to n = 1000, and the finite-criterion thresholds) and extensions.py (the table of limit values and the interval certificates of the explicit failures in ranks two, three and four). A clean replay in Python's optimised mode reproduced both recorded outputs; altering the constant 2401/1800 or tightening the certificate threshold makes the programs fail; Linux CI reruns them. Proposition 2.9 rests on the interval certificates; elsewhere the programs are cross-checks.

keyResults: Theorem 2.2 (proof): for fixed ℓ ≥ 2 and k ≥ 2, A(ℓ,n,k) = (n!/k!) β n^{k(ℓ−1)−1}[S(n) + O((1+log n)^k/n)] with a bounded Euler-product singular series S and a constant uniform in the factorisation of n; Theorem 2.6 makes the error explicit.
Theorem 2.3 (proof): Abdesselam's conjecture fails at two orbits in every rank: R_{ℓ,2}(m!) → 0, and R_{ℓ,2} < ε on all large multiples of some Q.

Theorems 2.4 and 2.5 (proof): at every fixed k ≥ 3 log-concavity holds for large n; the exact lim inf and lim sup are Euler products, about 2.52 at ℓ = 3, k = 3 against the elementary bound 1.10, reproducing Starr's formula at rank two.
Theorem 2.8 (proof): the ratio has a continuous limiting distribution, so the density of two-orbit failures exists and lies strictly between 0 and 1 in every rank, new also at rank two.
Proposition 2.9 (interval certificate): explicit failures with a 54-digit n (about 1.45 × 10^53) for three commuting permutations and an 845-digit n for four; neither is claimed minimal.

Limits and credit: fixed orbit counts only; the leading term follows the Ingham–Halberstam route and the density applies the Erdős–Wintner theorem; the rank-two cases are due to Starr and to Charlton, Heim and Stumpenhusen.
